newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK democrats urge Tung to sway China on democracy.
newsitem.headline: HK democrats urge Tung to sway China on democracy.

text.p: Hong Kong's Democratic Party urged the territory's post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa on Friday to convince China there was nothing to fear from the free rein of human rights and democracy.

Party leader Martin Lee issued the call as the democracy camp launched protests against a Chinese plan to scrap a clutch of laws on civil liberties and reinstate old laws placing curbs on the freedom of association after Beijing takes over in July.
"I think he should explain to the Chinese leaders that there is nothing to fear about our existing laws," Lee said.
"Mr Tung should defend Hong Kong's system, a system which works so well for our people. He should explain that to China," he told a news conference. "He should keep the present law."
A legal subgroup of the China-controlled Preparatory Committee last Sunday proposed scrapping liberal political laws enacted in the twilight years of British rule.
The group said changes were warranted because the laws contravened the Basic Law, the territory's post-colonial constitution promulgated by Beijing in 1990.
Legislation facing the axe includes parts of the Bill of Rights and laws allowing freedom of assembly and association.

After more than 150 years of colonial rule, Britain hands back Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30 under a 1984 treaty in which China vowed to keep the territory's capitalist system and way of life for a further half century.

On Thursday, Tung said the proposals did not involve human rights but were a matter of weighing freedoms against responsibilities. He also said other states required permits for rallies and set limits on overseas links of political groups.

"We are very disappointed with the speech delivered by Mr Tung last night because he said that the key issues which are causing so much concern in Hong Kong arising from the recommendations of the legal subgroup...have nothing to do with human rights and have nothing to do with law," Lee said.
"We believe these problems have everything to do with human rights and everything to do with law."
Lee is due to set off on an eight-nation tour of Europe on Sunday to lobby for support for human rights in post-handover Hong Kong.
Earlier, activists donned dunce caps aping China's Cultural Revolution antics as the democracy movement began a series of protests against Beijing's plans to curb civil liberties in the territory.
